passages.section: The algebraic PCP theorem: a detailed account of the Lean proof
passages.quote: The PCP theorem [AS98, ALMSS98] states that every language in NP has a polynomial-time verifier using $O(\log n)$ random bits and $O(1)$ proof-bit queries, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most one half.

Fix a target $a\in F^k$. The local corrector queries a points table $f$ with affine labels and the lines-table entries $f'_{a,v}$ of the lines through $a$. It chooses a uniform slope $v\in F^k$, a uniform parameter $z\in F^\times$, a uniform homogeneous label $L$, a slope in $F^{cb}$ for standard local correction, and an independent seed for the inner low-degree test. It runs the inner low-degree test on $f'_{a,v}$ and rejects if that test fails. Otherwise it corrects the entry at $\Phi(z)$ by (B12) and compares the answer with $f(a+zv,L)$, rejecting if they differ. If both checks pass, it returns the correction at $\Phi(0)$, computed with the same inner slope and label.

anchor.heading: 3.10 The reduction from NP to three-colourability

passages.quote: A constraint over an alphabet of size $A$ is converted to Boolean constraints by one-hot coding. Each source variable receives $A$ bits, exactly one of which is true; its true index is the encoded symbol. Validity constraints enforce this condition. A relation inspects the relevant one-hot blocks and accepts precisely the tuples accepted by the original finite relation. The alphabet size and local arity are constants fixed by the original machine. Reading the true indices of a satisfying one-hot assignment, and encoding a source assignment, both preserve all constraints.

anchor.heading: 3.10 The reduction from NP to three-colourability

passages.quote: To encode NAE by a graph, make a palette triangle with colours $0,1,2$. Each Boolean variable has two adjacent vertices, one for itself and one for its negation; both are joined to palette vertex 2. They must therefore receive complementary colours 0 and 1. Constant literals 0 and 1 use the corresponding palette vertices. For a NAE clause, make a new triangle and join its $i$-th vertex to the vertex for its $i$-th literal. If the three literal colours are equal, every vertex of the new triangle is forbidden that colour, so three distinct colours are impossible. If the literals are not all equal, the triangle can be coloured: for literal colours $(0,0,1)$, use triangle colours $(1,2,0)$; complementing or permuting yields the other cases. A colouring of the whole graph can first be relabelled so the palette has colours 0,1,2, after which it yields a satisfying Boolean assignment.

anchor.heading: 3.10 The reduction from NP to three-colourability

passages.quote: **Proposition 3.13 (reduction to three-colourability).** For every NP language $\mathcal L$ there are a map $f$ on bit strings, a polynomial $p_f\in\mathbb N[X]$, a program and constants $C,e$, depending only on the witness relation, its length bound and its checker, such that for every input $x$ the program emits $f(x)$ at charged cost at most $C(|x|+1)^e$, the output has length at most $p_f(|x|)$, and $G_{f(x)}$ is three-colourable if and only if $x\in\mathcal L$.
